name: Whitening mouth rinse

lead: Whitening rinses are over-the-counter mouthwashes containing a peroxide, used to lighten tooth colour and reduce surface stain with very little effort.

The peroxide oxidises stain molecules on the teeth, though contact time is short compared with strips or trays, so results are described as gradual. Published work on rinses is mostly laboratory studies, case reports and product analyses rather than clinical trials of cosmetic whitening.

paras: Users swish the rinse as part of the daily routine, twice daily for about a minute each time in the usual description. Visible results can take up to three months.
One case report documents a chemical gum burn after misuse. Peroxide at 10 percent or more is described as able to burn tissue, and EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.

angle.text: A peroxide rinse contacts the teeth twice a day and gradually lifts surface stain, giving a slightly brighter smile over weeks to a few months. It is the lowest-effort whitening option; supporting research is mainly laboratory work.

lead: Whitening mouth rinses are over-the-counter mouthwashes containing a peroxide intended to lighten tooth colour or reduce stain. Wikipedia lists rinses among at-home whitening methods, describing use twice daily for one minute each time, with visible results that can take up to three months.[1]
Evidence available for this article consists mostly of laboratory studies, case reports and product analyses rather than clinical trials of cosmetic whitening.

paras: Whitening rinses are swished in the mouth rather than held against the teeth, so peroxide contact time is brief compared with strips or trays.[1] Wikipedia lists rinses alongside strips, brush-on gels and trays as home options.[1] A laboratory study of whitening rinses tested a peroxide product (Rembrandt Plus) against alcohol-containing and alcohol-free mouthwashes.[2]

No studies found. Related laboratory work: studies have examined how whitening rinses affect the surface hardness, gloss and colour of bleached composite resin, bulk-fill composites, and composite aligner attachments stained with coffee and wine.[2][3][4] A laboratory analysis of 16 commercial whitening products also compared the real and declared concentrations of hydrogen peroxide.[5]

A case report described a chemical burn to the gum after misuse of an over-the-counter whitening mouthwash.[6] Wikipedia notes that hydrogen peroxide at 10 percent or more can cause chemical burns, and that EU retail products are limited to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide.[1]
